promise: After this you can explain what CAP forces you to choose, how R, W and N tune that choice, and what each side costs.

terms.definition: One of several copies of the same data kept on different machines.
A break that stops some nodes from reaching others, even though each is still running.
Consistency means every read sees the latest write; availability means every request gets a non-error answer.

before.note: Read Replication and Sharding first: CAP is about what happens to replicated, partitioned data when the network between copies breaks. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: Once data lives on more than one machine, the network between those machines can fail: messages are dropped or delayed, and two groups of nodes can no longer talk. That is a network partition. The CAP theorem is about what a system does in that moment. Our summary of it, which none of the cited pages states: during a partition you can keep every node answering (availability) or keep every answer correct and up to date (consistency), but not both at once.

General background, not from a cited page: the popular shorthand "pick two of three: consistency, availability, partition tolerance" is misleading. On a real network, partitions happen whether you want them or not, so partition tolerance is not something you trade away. The honest statement is: when a partition occurs, choose consistency or availability. When there is no partition, a good system gives you both.

Different databases make this choice differently, and often make it configurable. Amazon's DynamoDB, for instance, offers two read modes: eventually consistent reads (the default), which Amazon notes might not reflect a recently completed write, and strongly consistent reads, which do but cost more [[aws-ddb-consistency]]. That single setting is the CAP trade-off made concrete.

terms.definition: During a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability.
Continuing to operate despite dropped or delayed messages; mandatory on a real network.
A read that may not yet reflect the newest write, but will once replicas converge.
A read guaranteed to reflect the latest acknowledged write.

That Cassandra offers a per-operation tradeoff between consistency and availability through consistency levels.

stages.name: How it works
body: The common way to make the CAP choice adjustable is a quorum over replicas. Apache Cassandra describes its consistency levels as a version of Dynamo's R + W > N mechanism: with a replication factor N, the operator sets how many nodes must take part in reads (R) and writes (W). The page says that when the read level contains enough nodes to guarantee a quorum intersection with the write level, writes will generally be visible to subsequent reads [[cassandra-dynamo]]. The overlap alone is not the whole of strong consistency: concurrent writes still need an order, and a sloppy quorum, which accepts writes on stand-in nodes, does not give the overlap at all.

That overlap is the knob. High R and W give the overlap that strong consistency needs but require more replicas reachable, so a partition that isolates too many nodes makes the operation fail: the consistent, less-available end. Low R and W let reads and writes succeed with fewer replicas, so the system keeps answering through a partition but can return stale data: the available, less-consistent end. Cassandra lets you choose this per operation through consistency levels, without even knowing the replication factor [[cassandra-dynamo]].

The far consistent end is a system that keeps one correct global order no matter what. Google Spanner does this: it uses TrueTime, a highly available distributed clock, to assign transaction timestamps, and provides external consistency, its strictest guarantee: the system behaves as if transactions ran one after another, in an order that matches the order in which they can be observed to commit [[spanner-truetime]]. The page notes that proper timestamping is trivial on a single machine and much harder to do efficiently across a widely distributed system, which is the problem TrueTime addresses.

terms.definition: How many replicas hold each piece of data.
How many replicas must answer a read (R) or acknowledge a write (W).
Cassandra's term for a read set and a write set that share a replica, so a read reaches a replica that has the acknowledged write.
A per-operation setting that picks R and W behaviour, trading consistency against availability and latency.
The strictest guarantee: transactions appear in an order consistent with real time.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: If you keep the system available during a partition, two sides can accept writes that the other never sees, so the copies diverge and must be reconciled when the partition heals. Cassandra converges replicas using mutation-timestamp versioning, so a later write wins over an earlier one [[cassandra-dynamo]]. Cassandra calls this a simpler last-write-wins model than the vector clocks of the original Dynamo paper, and the latest version is the winning value, so the other mutation does not win. Systems that cannot accept that loss can instead keep both versions and let the application merge them.

If you keep the system consistent instead, the cost moves to coordination. Spanner's page says that under external consistency the system behaves as if all transactions ran sequentially, even though they run across many servers and possibly datacenters, and that this needs timestamps assigned with TrueTime [[spanner-truetime]]. The reward is that application developers do not see states that break the order transactions committed in; the page gives no latency figures, so measure the cost on your own system.

Either way, the choice is best made per piece of data, not once for the whole system. DynamoDB exposes exactly this: the same table can be read eventually consistent or strongly consistent per request, and eventually consistent reads cost half as much [[aws-ddb-consistency]]. Pick the cheaper, available mode where staleness is harmless, and the stronger mode where it is not.

terms.definition: Merging replica versions that diverged during a partition, by last-write-wins or application logic.
A simple conflict rule that keeps the most recent write and discards the other, which can lose data.
Spanner's term for giving transactions timestamps that match the order in which they can be observed to commit.
How long after a write a read might still return the old value under eventual consistency.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: In practice the first question for any stored data is: if a partition hit right now, would you rather this request fail or return possibly stale data? A shopping cart or a product view can tolerate staleness and should stay available; a bank balance or an inventory count cannot tolerate two disagreeing truths and should refuse rather than diverge. The same database can serve both by setting the consistency level per operation [[cassandra-dynamo]].

Watch for the hidden costs on each side. On the available side, eventual consistency is cheaper and faster, but you must build and test the reconciliation path and accept a staleness window; Amazon makes the cost explicit by charging eventually consistent reads at half the price of strongly consistent ones [[aws-ddb-consistency]]. On the consistent side, you pay in coordination, and at global scale you depend on something like Spanner's TrueTime clock service [[spanner-truetime]].

The deepest practical point is that CAP applies per operation and per kind of data: it is a decision about what to do during the partitions that will happen, so one database can answer differently for different data. Decide it deliberately for each kind of data, measure the staleness or the latency you are paying, and revisit it as the data's needs change.

terms.definition: One that favours availability during partitions, staying up but possibly stale.
One that favours consistency during partitions, refusing rather than serving unsafe data.
Setting consistency per request so one store can serve both AP and CP workloads.
A middle guarantee where a client at least sees its own latest writes, even if others lag.

reading.what: How to choose a per-operation level for a given data need, including LOCAL_QUORUM and ONE.

misconceptions.myth: CAP means pick any two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.
misconceptions.truth: Partitions are unavoidable on a real network, so the real choice is consistency versus availability while a partition is happening.

misconceptions.myth: A database is permanently either consistent or available.
misconceptions.truth: Cassandra describes a per-operation tradeoff through consistency levels [[cassandra-dynamo]], and DynamoDB lets you choose eventually or strongly consistent reads per request [[aws-ddb-consistency]].

misconceptions.myth: Eventual consistency means the data is just wrong.
misconceptions.truth: DynamoDB says that repeating an eventually consistent read after a short time should eventually return the more recent item [[aws-ddb-consistency]].

misconceptions.myth: Strong consistency across the globe is free if you engineer well.
misconceptions.truth: The Spanner page says proper timestamping is much harder to do efficiently in a widely distributed system, and Spanner relies on TrueTime for it [[spanner-truetime]].

tryIt.intro: These use cqlsh, the shell for Apache Cassandra, against a local or test cluster, to see a per-operation consistency level. CONSISTENCY is a cqlsh special command, QUORUM and ONE are levels the Cassandra pages list, and the SELECT is a query shown on the cqlsh page. Output depends on your cluster, so it is not shown here.

commands.shows: Sets the consistency level for the operations that follow to QUORUM, a majority of the replicas (the consistent end).
Sets the level to ONE, where only a single replica must respond (the available end).
A read of a system table, answered under whichever consistency level the session is set to.

next: Go back to the CAP Theorem topic page for the worked example and the quiz, then read the Dynamo and Spanner papers for the two opposite choices made in production. CAP leads into Consensus, where a majority of replicas agree on one order so a system can stay consistent as long as a quorum survives.
